extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent applicants and their counsel (patent attorneys/agents), inventors preparing USPTO filings
extracted.subtask_description: Preparing and submitting an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) to the USPTO: identifying and disclosing all known prior art and relevant information, meeting timing/fee rules under 37 CFR § 1.56, and avoiding inequitable-conduct risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor and good faith (37 CFR § 1.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 CFR § 1.56, patent applicants have a duty of candor and good faith, which means they must disclose any prior art or information that is material to the examination of the patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO requires applicants to disclose any known prior art or relevant information, whether favorable or unfavorable. This statutory/regulatory duty is the baseline obligation that makes IDS submission important.

rubrics_metrics.name: What Information Should Be Included in an IDS
rubrics_metrics.description: An IDS must disclose all relevant prior art and information known to the applicant, including patents and published patent applications, non-patent literature, third-party submissions, and related litigation information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically include: US and foreign patents or applications related to the invention; scientific articles, technical papers, research reports, etc. (non-patent literature); information submitted by third parties that is relevant to patentability; and documents from ongoing lawsuits involving the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to File an IDS (deadlines and fee consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: An IDS can be filed at different stages of the patent application process, but there are strict deadlines and fee consequences depending on timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing windows and fees as stated: (1) With the initial application filing — no fee required. (2) Within three months of filing or before the first Office action — no fee required. (3) After the first Office action but before a final Office action or Notice of Allowance — a small fee is required. (4) After Notice of Allowance — requires a petition and an additional fee, and must include a statement confirming the information was discovered after the earlier IDS deadline. File promptly to avoid extra fees/complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failing to disclose relevant prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to disclose relevant prior art could result in patent invalidation, allegations of inequitable conduct, or the patent being deemed unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant intentionally withholds material prior art, courts may find fraud or misrepresentation, making the patent unenforceable. During litigation, competitors may argue failure to disclose relevant prior art, weakening enforceability and exposing the patent to invalidity challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding inequitable conduct claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Timely and complete IDS submission helps avoid claims of fraud or misrepresentation (inequitable conduct) that can render a patent unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose material references even if unfavorable. Failure to disclose material information may lead to allegations of inequitable conduct; therefore, candid disclosure reduces risk of such claims in prosecution and litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefit: strengthening the patent's validity by disclosing prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: By disclosing all relevant prior art, the patent becomes less vulnerable to invalidity challenges in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thorough IDS makes later attacks on validity harder by putting the examiner on notice and creating a clear prosecution record. Proper IDS submission helps protect the validity and enforceability of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptness and completeness as practical guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: An IDS must be filed promptly and must be complete with all relevant known information to avoid fees, complications, or exposure to legal challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: file known references early (ideally with the initial filing or within three months) to avoid fees and reduce risk. If new material is discovered after deadlines, be prepared to file in the appropriate later window and, if after allowance, supply the required petition and statement explaining the timing.
